prompt:
Write an opinion piece of about 800 words on whether cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.

text:
Cities should scrap their minimum parking requirements, and they should do it soon, because the rules force every new building to subsidize car storage whether or not anyone who lives or works there owns a car. A minimum parking requirement says that a restaurant must provide so many spaces per hundred square feet, an apartment building so many per unit, a medical office so many per thousand square feet, and the numbers in most codes were not derived from careful study of local demand. Many were borrowed from a handbook of trip-generation rates compiled by traffic engineers, who measured peak demand at suburban sites where parking was free and plentiful, and then written into law as though those peaks were the minimum any city should tolerate on an ordinary day. The result is a built environment sized for the busiest hour of the busiest day of the year, which means that for most of the year a great deal of expensive land sits empty.

That land is not free, and neither is the concrete on it. A surface space costs a few thousand dollars to build once you count paving, drainage and lighting, and a space in a structure or underground garage can run from thirty thousand dollars to well over fifty thousand in a high-cost city. Developers do not absorb that cost out of generosity; they pass it into rents and sale prices, and the household that owns no car pays for the garage anyway. Research on apartment buildings has repeatedly found that required parking raises the cost of a unit by a meaningful fraction, and in some projects the requirement is what tips a modest building from marginal to unbuildable. A city that says it wants more housing and also demands two spaces per home is asking for two incompatible things, and the parking rule is the one that wins, because it is written in the code and enforced at the permit counter.

The damage reaches well beyond housing costs. Small commercial buildings on small lots are often impossible to renovate or convert, because a change of use triggers a fresh calculation of required spaces that the lot cannot physically hold; the corner building that was a shop for eighty years cannot become a café because the café needs more parking than the shop did and there is nowhere to put it. Historic downtowns, which were built before these rules and which tend to be the most walkable and financially productive land in a region, are effectively illegal to build again under current law. Meanwhile the parking that does get built spreads buildings apart, lengthens walking distances, and makes transit and walking less practical for everyone, which in turn makes the cars that the parking was meant to serve more necessary, so the rule partly manufactures the demand it claims merely to meet.

The most common objection is that without requirements, developers will build too little parking and the surrounding streets will fill with the cars of residents and customers. This worry deserves a serious answer, and the answer is that removing a minimum does not remove parking, it removes the compulsion. Developers who expect their tenants or customers to drive will keep building spaces, because buildings without parking where parking is wanted rent for less, and lenders know it. What changes is that a project near a train station, or aimed at students or seniors or people who have chosen not to own a car, can build fewer spaces and charge less, while a suburban shopping center can still provide a sea of them. The decision moves from a formula in the code to the person putting up the money and bearing the risk, who usually knows the site better than a regulator working from a national table.

Where spillover onto public streets does become a problem, the right tool is to price and manage the curb rather than to force private owners to oversupply their own lots. Residential permit districts, meters that rise in price until a space or two is always open, and revenue returned to the neighborhood that generates it all address congestion directly, and they treat street space as the scarce public resource it is instead of as a free good that new buildings must be forced to protect. Cities that have tried this have generally found that the dire predictions did not arrive on schedule. Buffalo eliminated its minimums citywide in 2017, and Minneapolis, Seattle, and a growing list of cities in the United States and abroad have followed in various forms, and the sky has stayed where it was while developers have proposed more projects on lots that previously could not pencil out. California, Oregon and other states have begun to override local requirements near transit, which suggests that the idea has moved from fringe proposal to mainstream practice.

None of this means that parking is bad or that cars should be hounded out of cities. People will go on driving, and plenty of buildings will go on including generous parking because their owners judge that it pays. The argument is only about who gets to decide, and about whether a number invented by a committee should override the judgment of the person paying for the building and the market that will rent it. A fair rule would let those who want parking build it and those who do not build without it, and would deal with any genuine street-level congestion through pricing instead of mandates. A city that keeps its minimums is choosing, whether it intends to or not, higher housing costs, emptier storefronts, and wider seas of asphalt, and it is making that choice on behalf of residents who were never asked. Repealing the requirement costs the public treasury nothing and gives builders and neighborhoods room to adapt, which is about as cheap and as effective as a reform in urban policy ever gets.
